name: Fractional laser resurfacing

card.summary: Clinic laser that treats skin in tiny columns to remodel scars and texture; well studied for scars and photoaging, with real downtime.
card.aka: Fraxel, fractional CO2, ablative fractional laser
card.note: Ablative versions involve days of visible wounding and recovery; pigment and scarring complications are documented, especially in darker skin types.

quick.overview:
Fractional laser resurfacing uses a laser that treats a grid of microscopic columns of skin and leaves the tissue between them intact. It is offered by dermatologists and plastic surgeons for acne scars, other scars, wrinkles, sun damage and uneven texture.

In looksmaxxing communities it sits in the clinic-based 'hardmaxx' tier of skin treatment. Forum users describe it as a stronger option than at-home skincare, and some report that recovery is harder than expected.
quick.mechanism: Ablative lasers (such as CO2 and erbium) vaporize microscopic channels of skin, while non-ablative fractional lasers heat the tissue without removing it. The resulting controlled injury is described in the literature as stimulating new collagen and remodeling of the dermis. Because only a fraction of the surface is treated each time, healing is faster than with older fully ablative resurfacing.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects include redness, swelling, crusting, acne flares, herpes simplex reactivation, pigment changes and scarring. Dermatology reviews describe skin phototyping (the Fitzpatrick scale) as relevant to predicting outcomes of procedures such as laser resurfacing. Treatments are performed by licensed clinicians; devices are regulated medical devices in most jurisdictions.

lead: Fractional laser resurfacing is a cosmetic and medical procedure in which a laser delivers energy to the skin in a pattern of many microscopic zones, leaving untreated skin between them. It is used for scars (especially atrophic acne scars), wrinkles, sun-damaged skin, stretch marks and uneven texture, and is a form of the broader category of laser skin resurfacing. [1][2]

Fractional devices come in two main kinds. Ablative systems, typically CO2 or erbium lasers, vaporize tissue in the treated columns; non-ablative systems, such as the 1550 nm devices marketed as Fraxel, heat the dermis without removing the surface. [1][3] Fractional treatment was developed after earlier fully ablative CO2 resurfacing, which produced notable results but also high complication rates. [3][4]

Clinical studies, consensus reports and randomized trials support fractional laser treatment for several scar types, with improvement typically gradual over multiple sessions. Reported adverse effects include prolonged redness, pigment changes, infection and scarring, and downtime for ablative treatments is several days. [5][6][7] Forum users on looksmax.org discuss it as a clinic option within skin-focused looksmaxxing and describe heavy downtime. [8]

paras: Laser resurfacing is divided into ablative methods, which vaporize tissue and create a wound, and non-ablative methods, which leave the skin surface intact. Fractional delivery places many small treated zones per area of skin with healthy tissue between them, which is intended to speed healing compared with treating the whole surface. [9][3]

Reviews of the field describe a spectrum running from non-ablative fractional lasers, through ablative fractional CO2 and erbium devices, to fully ablative resurfacing, with a trade-off between degree of change and recovery time. [3]

Clinicians commonly classify skin by the Fitzpatrick scale, which is based on tendency to burn and tan, because it relates to the risk of photodamage and to outcomes after procedures such as laser resurfacing and chemical peeling. [10] A registered trial of a 1550 nm fractional laser for acne scars was specifically designed for Fitzpatrick types IV to VI. [11]

Conventional lasers resurfaced the whole treated area. Fractional photothermolysis instead creates thousands of narrow microscopic columns of thermal injury, each surrounded by intact tissue. Because the untreated skin around each column acts as a reservoir of cells, the surface can close over quickly, which is why healing is faster than after full-field ablative resurfacing.[1][36]

The body responds to the controlled injury by remodelling the dermis: damaged collagen is replaced and new collagen and elastin are laid down over the following weeks and months. Researchers who study ageing skin describe fibroblast collapse, in which fibroblasts lose their mechanical tension and produce less collagen, as one feature of looking older, and laser and other resurfacing procedures are discussed as ways of re-stimulating those cells.[7]

Practitioners choose depth and density according to the goal. Superficial, non-ablative settings are used for fine lines, tone and mild texture, usually across a series of sessions with little downtime. Deeper ablative fractional CO2 or erbium treatment is used for pronounced wrinkles, acne scars and burn scars, with longer recovery and, as reviews report, a more pronounced change per session.[3][35]

Laser resurfacing began in the 1980s with continuous-wave CO2 lasers, whose high rate of side effects including scarring led to the development of short-pulse, rapidly scanned CO2 lasers and erbium:YAG lasers. [3] A 1996 study of pulsed CO2 resurfacing in 111 perioral and periorbital areas reported clinical improvement in photoaged skin, and a 1998 evaluation of 500 patients catalogued complications of the technique. [12][4]

A 2007 study applied fractional photothermolysis to atrophic scars. [13] A 2014 consensus report addressed laser treatment of traumatic scars with an emphasis on ablative fractional resurfacing. [14] A 2008 report on 961 fractional treatments described the side-effect profile of the newer technique. [15]

The concept of fractional photothermolysis was described in 2004 by Dieter Manstein, G. Scott Herron, R. Kehl Sink, Henry Tanner and R. Rox Anderson in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine. Their prototype 1.5 micrometre devices were tested on the forearms of 15 volunteers and on photoaged periorbital skin in 30 more; treated zones were about 100 micrometres wide and 300 micrometres deep, the surface re-epithelialised within a day, and wrinkle scores improved by 18 percent at three months.[39]

The Fraxel brand was developed by Reliant Technologies from 2004, using a patent licensed from the Wellman Center for Photomedicine at Massachusetts General Hospital; R. Rox Anderson is named as inventor.[32] The first product, a non-ablative 1,550 nm erbium-glass laser, was followed by dual-wavelength systems that add a 1,927 nm thulium laser and by ablative 10,600 nm CO2 versions.[32][33] Competing manufacturers later introduced their own fractional CO2 and erbium platforms, so that "fractional laser" now names a category rather than a single device.
Fractional laser sits within the wider field of photorejuvenation, which also includes intense pulsed light, radiofrequency and photodynamic approaches.[34]

A 2015 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery review dates the introduction of ablative fractional resurfacing to 2007, describes how the approach grew out of observations on lasers designed for hair transplantation, and says fractionation allowed deeper penetration with greater tissue contraction and collagen production.[36] The same review says fractional systems let surgeons treat higher Fitzpatrick skin types (IV to VI) and tailor treatment to individual facial subunits by adjusting microspot density, pulse duration, number of passes and fluence.[36]

Fraxel Restore is a non-ablative 1,550 nm erbium-glass system described as the gentlest of the line, used for texture, mild wrinkles, photoaging and mild acne scarring. Fraxel Restore Dual adds an ablative 1,927 nm thulium fibre laser and is used for wrinkles, photoaging, surgical and acne scars, while Fraxel Repair uses an ablative 10,600 nm CO2 laser and is often applied to wrinkles around the mouth and eyes.[32] Other manufacturers sell fractional CO2 and erbium platforms, so clinicians talk about the category by wavelength and mode rather than by brand.[36]

A 2009 review of non-ablative fractional resurfacing describes it as preserving the stratum corneum, producing microscopic thermal zones that lead to new collagen formation, and giving the most impressive results for acne scars, surgical and traumatic scars, and mild to moderate dyschromia or photoaging, with modest results for therapy-resistant melasma and certain wrinkles.[35]

Treatment is performed in a clinic by a physician or trained clinician. Reviews of the field describe that practitioners adjust density, depth and number of passes to the target, and that non-ablative treatment is typically repeated across a series of sessions while ablative treatment is used less often but has more downtime.[3][35][36]

The 2015 review states that fractional lasers have a short recovery time compared with earlier fully ablative resurfacing, allowing patients to resume regular activities more quickly, while noting a relatively high safety profile for ablative fractionated lasers with continued need for surgeon awareness of complications.[36] Post-treatment care is described in the non-ablative literature as a core part of managing complications and speeding healing, and a 2025 split-face randomized trial in a Chinese population tested a vitamin C, vitamin E and ferulic acid serum after non-ablative Fraxel treatment.[35][19]

People who have had ablative treatment describe the experience in less clinical terms. One looksmax.org poster titled a thread on CO2 resurfacing as brutal, saying they stayed indoors and avoided weight training for about a week and were advised to have three sessions.[8]

Fractional laser is often combined with other measures. A 2016 treatment-algorithm review in Dermatologic Surgery proposed combining surgical-scar treatments, listing pulse dye laser, non-ablative and ablative fractional resurfacing, microneedling, injections and excision, used alone or together.[40] Trials and reports have examined fractional CO2 followed by photodynamic therapy for actinic keratosis, hyaluronic acid for acne scars, platelet-rich plasma and botulinum toxin combinations.[20][21][22][23]

Fractional lasers are medical devices. They are used under a clinician's supervision in dermatology and plastic-surgery practice, and device types are regulated in the jurisdictions where they are sold, as described in the general laser resurfacing literature.[9] Wikipedia's article on laser resurfacing also records a 2010 study suggesting heat exposure may damage DNA in nearby unheated cells, with authors calling for more research.[9]

Human studies cover several indications. A randomized trial compared fractional CO2 laser with carboxytherapy for stretch marks. [16] Fractional CO2 has been studied for acne scarring, where a 2008 report described successful treatment of acneiform scars, and for burn scars, where a 2022 review concluded laser therapy is superior to topical treatments and can be combined with surgery. [17][18]

Randomized and controlled trials have tested fractional laser combined with other treatments, including a split-face trial of an antioxidant serum after non-ablative fractional laser in a Chinese population, a trial of fractional CO2 followed by photodynamic therapy for actinic keratosis, and combinations with platelet-rich plasma, hyaluronic acid and botulinum toxin. [19][20][21][22][23] A randomized trial of fractionated laser on aged skin was also run to test whether it could reduce later actinic neoplasia, with related trials registered. [24][25]

Complication data come mostly from case series: the 500-patient CO2 series and the 961-treatment fractional series. [4][15] Trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies of a 2910 nm laser for perioral lines and of self-harm scars. [26][27]

Reviews comparing laser types report a consistent pattern: non-ablative fractional treatment gives milder, more gradual improvement in photoaging and scars with minimal downtime, while ablative fractional treatment gives larger improvements with more downtime and a higher complication risk.[3][35][36] Registered trials have examined fractional laser combined with platelet-rich plasma for post-acne scars and fractional CO2 for facial freckles.[37][38]

Reported effects after fractional or ablative resurfacing include erythema, swelling, crusting, acne eruptions, herpes simplex outbreaks, changes in pigmentation and scarring. [15][4][9] CO2 lasers have been described as carrying a greater risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers because of greater heat generation. [9]

A 2023 review of chemical peels characterized lasers as having proved inadequate for some deep perioral lines, in contrast to deep peels. [28] A review of burn scars notes that the use of lasers in hospital dermatology departments remains limited. [18]

Fractional resurfacing appears in looksmax.org discussions as a clinic-based treatment for skin. One user described having CO2 resurfacing and being unable to go outside or exercise for about a week afterward, and said three sessions had been recommended. [8] Other posters in the same thread discussed laser hair removal and intense pulsed light as skin-improvement options. [8] Users also list laser resurfacing as one of several procedures bundled in surgery trips abroad. [29]

In appearance communities the procedure is usually grouped with other skin-quality interventions such as retinoids, chemical peels and microneedling. Participants who describe ablative treatment mention the roughly week-long period when they could not go out or exercise, and a recommendation of multiple sessions.[8] Posters who combine it with surgical work abroad, such as one who listed laser skin resurfacing alongside other procedures on a medical-tourism trip, add a travel dimension; a 2024 review addresses the challenges of medical tourism.[29][31]

Ongoing registered trials examine fractional laser as prophylaxis against actinic keratosis and non-melanoma skin cancer in older skin, laser-induced rejuvenation mechanisms, and newer wavelengths. [24][25][26][30]

timeline.event: Continuous-wave CO2 lasers introduced for resurfacing; high side-effect rates prompt newer designs. [3]
Study reports clinical improvement of photoaged perioral and periorbital skin with a pulsed CO2 laser. [12]
Evaluation of complications in 500 patients treated with CO2 laser resurfacing is published. [4]
Manstein, Anderson and colleagues describe fractional photothermolysis; Reliant Technologies introduces the Fraxel line the same year.[39][32]
Fractional photothermolysis studied for atrophic scars. [13]
Ablative fractional laser resurfacing is introduced, per a 2015 review.[36]
Side effects of 961 fractional treatments reported. [15]
Review of non-ablative fractional resurfacing summarises indications and complications.[35]
Consensus report on laser treatment of traumatic scars with emphasis on ablative fractional resurfacing. [14]
JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery review describes fractional resurfacing for higher Fitzpatrick skin types.[36]
A looksmax.org thread describes CO2 laser resurfacing recovery.[8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, fractional laser is discussed as a stronger clinic alternative to skincare, with posters trading accounts of the downtime and the number of sessions needed. [8]

claims.claim: Clinic laser resurfacing meaningfully improves scars and skin texture.
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a heavy but worthwhile treatment and say people improve their skin from lasers and light treatments. [8]
claims.experts: Reviews and consensus reports support fractional laser for several scar types, with gradual improvement over multiple sessions. [14][18][17]

claims.claim: Recovery is brutal and needs about a week off.
claims.believers: One user reports a visibly injured face, staying indoors and not lifting weights for 7 days, with three sessions advised. [8]
claims.experts: Reviews describe days of erythema, crusting and healing after ablative resurfacing, with non-ablative devices involving shorter recovery. [3][9]

claims.claim: Lasers and light treatments such as IPL give long-lasting better skin overall.
claims.believers: A poster credits a series of IPL sessions with softer skin and says users 'massively improve' their skin from laser treatments. [8]
claims.experts: Published studies focus on specific indications such as scars, photoaging and pigment; no comparative trials of looksmaxxing-style skin outcomes were identified.

claims.claim: Laser resurfacing can be safely bundled into multi-procedure trips abroad.
claims.believers: One thread describes a trip combining laser resurfacing with several other procedures. [29]
claims.experts: Reviews of medical tourism report infectious and follow-up-care complications for patients treated abroad. [31]
